examples.name: Central Provident Fund (CPF)
what: Workers and their employers put part of each month's pay into the worker's CPF account.
The savings pay for retirement, a home and medical bills.
examples.shows: The government makes people save for their own needs, so the cost is shared between the person, the employer and the state.

examples.name: MediShield Life
what: A national health insurance scheme that began in 2015.
It covers every citizen and permanent resident for life, including those who are already ill.
It helps to pay large hospital bills.
examples.shows: The government spreads the cost of serious illness across everyone, so no one is left without cover.

examples.name: Electronic Road Pricing (ERP)
what: Since 1998, drivers pay a charge when they use busy roads at peak hours.
The charge is higher when the road is more crowded.
examples.shows: A policy can serve most people and still cost some people more: smoother roads for all, a higher cost for drivers.
use: deciding what is good for society

examples.name: NEWater
what: Used water is cleaned to a very high standard and used again.
The first NEWater plants opened in 2003.
It makes Singapore less dependent on rain and on water bought from abroad.
examples.shows: A government has to plan many years ahead for needs that are not urgent yet.

examples.name: REACH
what: The government's feedback unit. It started in 1985 and was renamed REACH in 2006.
It gathers views on policies through dialogues, surveys and online channels.
examples.shows: Citizens can shape policies by giving feedback, and the government has set up a channel to hear them.

examples.name: Our Singapore Conversation
what: A national series of dialogues held in 2012 and 2013.
More than 47,000 people took part and spoke about the future they wanted for the country.
examples.shows: Ordinary citizens were asked for their views before plans were made, so they had a part in setting priorities.

examples.name: Food from the Heart
what: A charity started in 2003.
Its volunteers collect unsold bread from bakeries and hotels and bring it to welfare homes and needy families.
It also gives out monthly food packs.
examples.shows: An organised group can meet a need that the government does not cover directly, by bringing many volunteers and donors together.

examples.name: Workfare Income Supplement
what: Since 2007, lower-wage Singaporean workers get a top-up from the government in cash and in CPF savings.
Older workers get more.
They get it only if they are working.
examples.shows: Help can be designed to reward work, so that people are supported without becoming dependent on aid.

examples.name: Ethnic Integration Policy
what: Since 1989, each public housing block and neighbourhood has a limit on the share of flats that each ethnic group can own.
examples.shows: The policy keeps people of different races living side by side, so that daily contact can build understanding.

examples.name: Racial Harmony Day
what: Schools mark it on 21 July each year, the date of the 1964 racial riots.
Students learn about one another's food, dress and customs.
examples.shows: Shared experiences from a young age help people to see other cultures as familiar and not strange.

examples.name: Harmony Circles (formerly IRCCs)
what: Inter-Racial Confidence Circles were set up in 2002 in every constituency.
Leaders of different races and religions meet, visit one another's places of worship and stand together in a crisis.
Since 2022 they are called Racial and Religious Harmony Circles.
examples.shows: Trust built in calm times lets community leaders calm tensions quickly when something goes wrong.

examples.name: Presidential Council for Minority Rights
what: Set up in 1970.
It checks new laws and reports to Parliament if a law would disadvantage a racial or religious community.
examples.shows: Minorities are protected by a safeguard in the law-making process itself.

examples.name: Group Representation Constituency (GRC)
what: Since 1988, candidates in a GRC stand for election as a team.
Each team must have at least one member from a minority community.
examples.shows: The system makes sure minority communities always have a voice in Parliament.

examples.name: Self-help groups
what: CDAC, Yayasan MENDAKI, SINDA and the Eurasian Association each serve one community.
They run low-cost tuition and give bursaries and help to families in need.
examples.shows: A group that shares a family's language and customs can reach it more easily. Some ask whether help by community keeps people apart.

examples.name: Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act
what: Passed in 1990.
It lets the Minister for Home Affairs issue a restraining order against a religious leader or member who stirs up ill-will between religious groups.
examples.shows: The law sets a firm limit, so that words that could divide people of different faiths can be stopped early.

examples.name: National Integration Council
what: Set up in 2009 to help newcomers and locals mix.
New citizens go through the Singapore Citizenship Journey, where they learn about the country's history and meet people in their community.
examples.shows: Integration is helped along by programmes that bring newcomers and locals together, and both sides have a part to play.

examples.name: Free trade agreements
what: Singapore has signed more than 20 free trade agreements with other countries and regions.
They lower taxes on goods traded between the partners.
examples.shows: Open trade gives firms here more customers abroad and gives people here more goods at lower prices.

examples.name: SkillsFuture
what: A national movement to help people keep learning through life.
From January 2016, Singaporeans aged 25 and above received $500 in credit to pay for approved courses.
examples.shows: Workers must keep learning to stay employable when jobs change or move abroad, and the government helps them to do so.

examples.name: Fair Consideration Framework
what: Since 2014, employers must consider Singaporeans fairly for jobs.
They must advertise a job opening on the national jobs portal before they apply to hire a foreign professional.
examples.shows: A country can stay open to foreign talent and still protect a fair chance for its own workers.

examples.name: Hawker culture on the UNESCO list
what: In December 2020, Singapore's hawker culture was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
examples.shows: A country can take steps to protect its own culture even as global brands and foreign food become common.

examples.name: A global chain with a local menu
what: In 2017, McDonald's in Singapore sold a nasi lemak burger.
Global chains often change their menus to suit local tastes.
examples.shows: Globalisation does not only replace local culture. Foreign and local ideas can mix into something new.

examples.name: The Jemaah Islamiyah plot
what: In December 2001, Singapore arrested members of a regional terror network, Jemaah Islamiyah.
They had planned to bomb embassies and other targets here.
examples.shows: Terror groups work across borders, so a small open country faces threats that begin outside it.

examples.name: SGSecure
what: A national movement launched in 2016.
It trains the public to stay alert, stay united and stay strong if a terror attack happens.
examples.shows: Security is not left to the government alone. Every person is asked to play a part.

examples.name: The SingHealth data breach
what: In 2018, hackers stole the personal data of about 1.5 million patients from SingHealth, a public healthcare group.
examples.shows: Being connected to the world through the internet brings new dangers, and attackers can strike from anywhere.
